hook: The child prodigy who wrote more than 600 works before he died at 35.

pages.x: Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756. His father Leopold, a court musician, saw that the boy could pick out chords at three and write music at five. From the age of six he toured the courts of Europe with his sister Nannerl, playing for kings and empresses.

At six he played for the empress Maria Theresa in Vienna. His father wrote that afterwards the boy jumped onto the empress's lap and kissed her. A later story says he slipped on the polished floor, and when the little princess Marie Antoinette helped him up, he said he would marry her.

At 14, in Rome, he heard Allegri's Miserere in the Sistine Chapel, a piece the Vatican did not allow to be copied. Back at his lodgings he wrote the whole thing out from memory, after hearing it just once.

He hated serving the Archbishop of Salzburg, who treated him like a servant. In 1781 he quit, and was thrown out with a kick from the archbishop's steward. He settled in Vienna as a freelance musician and married Constanze Weber.

Vienna loved anything Turkish, from coffee to the drums and cymbals of Turkish military bands. Around 1783 Mozart ended a piano sonata with a "Turkish march" that imitates them. It became one of his best known tunes.
In 1787 he wrote "A little night music", a serenade for strings, now one of the most famous pieces ever. It was not published until decades after his death.
In a single summer, in about six weeks, he wrote his last three symphonies, perhaps the greatest of his time. The restless No. 40 in G minor opens with this famous theme.

His operas The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni and The Magic Flute are still sung all over the world. In The Magic Flute, the furious Queen of the Night sings one of the hardest arias ever written, leaping to a very high F.

au.page: Der Hölle Rache kocht in meinem Herzen

pages.x: In 1791 a stranger ordered a Requiem, a mass for the dead, for a count who meant to pass it off as his own. Mozart, very ill, came to feel he was writing it for himself. He died at 35 with it unfinished. The tale that his rival Salieri poisoned him is false.
Mozart wrote more than 600 works in 35 years: symphonies, concertos, chamber music and operas that are still played somewhere in the world every day.
